A square $P Q R S$ with sides of length 10 is rolled without slipping along a line. Initially $P$ and $Q$ are on the line and the first roll is around point $Q$ as shown in the diagram. The rolling stops when $P$ first returns to the line. What is the length of the curve that $P$ has travelled?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First look at the image: in the figure, a square with side length 10 rolls to the right along a horizontal straight line without slipping; initially the bottom side PQ is on the straight line, then it flips in order around the contact points Q, R, S, until point P returns to the straight line again. Then reason: when rolling without slipping, point P travels along an arc around the current pivot in each flip, and each time it is 90°, that is, a quarter circle. The first time it goes around Q, with radius PQ=10, and the arc length is 10·(π/2). The second time it goes around R, with radius PR being the diagonal of the square, equal to 10√2, and the arc length is 10√2·(π/2). The third time it goes around S, with radius SP=10, and the arc length is 10·(π/2). The total length is 10(π/2)+10√2(π/2)+10(π/2)=10π+5π√2.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: the square starts with side PQ on the horizontal line, P at the left contact point and Q at the right contact point, and the arrow shows the square rolling clockwise about Q into successive positions to the right until P is again on the line. Use the visual sequence to identify the three quarter-turns before P returns to the ground: pivot about Q, then about R, then about S. From the text, take the side length as 10 and the motion as rolling without slipping. For each quarter-turn, compute the arc travelled by P about the current pivot: about Q the radius is PQ = 10; about R the radius is diagonal RP = 10√2; about S the radius is SP = 10. Each rotation is 90 degrees, so each arc length is radius times π/2. Sum: 10(π/2) + 10√2(π/2) + 10(π/2) = 10π + 5π√2.
